action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; here also the blood loss, hypoglycemia and blood alcohol [ACG_HE_2026]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Hold propranolol and diuretics during bleeding with hypotension; terlipressin can lower the sodium further (124 mEq/L); no relevant ceftriaxone interaction; thiamine before dextrose; avoid sedatives
action_criteria.label: Medication review: propranolol and diuretics in hemorrhagic shock, the vasoactive drug against the sodium, ceftriaxone, and sedatives
action_criteria.rationale: Active bleeding with hypotension, kidney injury and hyponatremia changes the safety of his beta-blocker and diuretics and the choice of vasoactive drug [Baveno_VII]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Hold propranolol during active hemorrhage with hypotension — blunts compensatory tachycardia.
Do not give NSAIDs (renal failure risk in cirrhosis).
Do not start protein restriction — outdated and harms outcomes.
Do not transfuse aggressively to normal Hgb — increases portal pressure and rebleeding.
required_recommendations: Start a vasoactive drug now (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide) and perform upper endoscopy with variceal band ligation within 12 hours of presentation, once resuscitated and with the airway protected (Baveno VII).
Transfuse PRBC to target Hgb 7-8 g/dL (over-transfusion worsens portal pressures).
Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily for SBP + bleeding cirrhotic antibiotic prophylaxis; IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3.

Lactulose by retention enema (300 mL in 700 mL water) every 4-6 hours until oral or nasogastric dosing is safe, then 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily by nasogastric tube.
Correct the glucose of 58 mg/dL with IV dextrose without delay, giving IV thiamine 500 mg first or with it (heavy alcohol use), and monitor capillary glucose.

Protect the airway: GCS 10 with a diminished gag reflex, agitation, active variceal bleeding and tense ascites; intubate for airway protection before endoscopy rather than waiting for a GCS below 8 (Baveno VII).
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Stop spironolactone and furosemide (hypotension, kidney injury, sodium 124 mEq/L); replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis; raise the sodium by no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours (alcohol use and malnutrition increase the risk of osmotic demyelination).

Monitor for alcohol withdrawal (heavy daily drinking up to admission, blood ethanol 168 mg/dL) and, if it develops, treat it symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).

Refer for liver transplant assessment once the bleed and SBP are controlled: decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, variceal bleeding and SBP, MELD-Na 38 (EASL 2018), together with treatment for alcohol use disorder (EASL ALD 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 38), precipitated by acute upper GI variceal hemorrhage (nitrogen load) plus spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 342) plus acute alcohol ingestion (ethanol 168).

differential.key_features: PMN 342, E. coli; treat empirically with ceftriaxone + albumin.
Coagulopathy (INR 3.2, platelets 56) and being found at home raise the question of an unwitnessed fall; the non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage, and there is no focal deficit.
Ethanol 168 mg/dL contributes; tolerant alcoholic so cannot fully account for GCS 10; monitor for withdrawal 24-72 h post-stop.
Creatinine 1.8 mg/dL with BUN 64 in hemorrhagic shock is pre-renal kidney injury; HRS-AKI cannot be diagnosed while shock persists; reassess after volume, albumin and control of bleeding.
High thiamine-deficiency risk; give empiric thiamine before any dextrose.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Upper GI bleed is one of the most potent HE precipitants — blood in gut is a massive nitrogen load; BUN/Cr ratio elevation supports an upper source.

Bacterial infection is present in about a fifth of patients with cirrhosis admitted with gastrointestinal bleeding, and SBP can coexist with a variceal bleed: both are treated at once, which is why every cirrhotic with variceal bleeding receives antibiotic prophylaxis (Baveno VII).
Restrictive transfusion strategy (Hgb 7-8) reduces rebleeding in variceal hemorrhage.
Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 18.6 3, albumin 1.8 3, INR 3.2 3, large-volume ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 38 (creatinine 1.8, bilirubin 18.6, INR 3.2, sodium 124, counted as 125)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol 168 cannot cause grade III obtundation with asterixis in a tolerant drinker; the liver failure with GI bleeding and SBP explains the encephalopathy, and the ammonia is supportive only.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute GCS 10 entirely to alcohol intoxication and observe.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diagnostic paracentesis is safe in Child-Pugh C with coagulopathy; prophylactic FFP/platelets are not required per AASLD.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 58-year-old man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 22 at his last clinic review) who was found confused and combative in his home by his adult son, who called 911. He could not be aroused to follow commands and had large amounts of tarry black stool on his clothing. His son found empty vodka bottles — the patient had been drinking. On presentation, he is hypotensive (BP 96/58), tachycardic (HR 124), with a temperature of 37.8°C. He has prominent jaundice, caput medusae, large-volume ascites, fetor hepaticus, and bilateral spider angiomata. Melena on rectal exam confirms active upper GI bleed. His neurological exam shows GCS 10 with prominent asterixis, disorientation, and bilateral Babinski signs.

neurological_exam.additional: Jaundice visible — sclerae and skin yellow. Spider angiomata on chest and shoulders. Caput medusae. Large-volume ascites. Fetor hepaticus — notable on entering room. Melena on rectal exam — active GI bleed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Extraocular movements intact. Gag reflex diminished.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to ambulate — too confused and uncooperative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 10 (E2V3M5). Confused and combative. Opens eyes to pain; responds to voice with inappropriate words. Localizes pain. Asterixis prominent bilaterally on arm extension. Disoriented — unable to state name correctly. Cannot follow any commands reliably.
neurological_exam.motor: Moving all extremities spontaneously. Tone increased. Occasional myoclonic jerks bilateral hands.
